story: Maya's class visited a fish farm by the coast on a windy morning. A guide explained that aquaculture is the farming of fish, shrimp, abalone, algae, and other seafood. In long ponds, workers raised catfish, salmon, and trout in clean, flowing water. The guide said aquaculture began in China a few thousand years ago, long before the modern tanks they saw. Maya fed pellets to young fish and watched them swirl in the tank, then wrote notes in her journal. Before they left, he showed a chart on the wall: aquaculture supplies over twenty percent of all seafood harvested worldwide. Maya had thought every fish came from the wild ocean. She walked back to the bus knowing that careful farming feeds many people around the world.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~126 words; covers all card facts.

story: Mr. Cole taught his class about abbreviations on a rainy afternoon. An abbreviation is a shorter way to write a word or phrase, and people use them for words they write often, like titles and addresses. Some abbreviations use an apostrophe, but many use periods instead, he said, tapping the board. Many English abbreviations come from Latin words, he added, opening an old grammar book. On the board he wrote i.e., which stands for id est and means that is. Below it he wrote e.g., from exempli gratia, meaning for example. Last he wrote et al., from et alii, meaning and others, for long lists of authors. A student used i.e. and e.g. correctly in one sentence. Mr. Cole smiled. The room was quiet, but everyone had learned three useful Latin shortcuts.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~132 words; covers all card facts.

story: In social studies, Ms. Park hung a map of the Middle East and asked what an Abrahamic religion is. She explained that it is a religion whose followers honor the prophet Abraham. Followers believe Abraham and his descendants play an important role in spiritual history, she said, pointing to dates on the timeline. The best-known Abrahamic religions are Judaism, Christianity, and Islam. Smaller traditions sometimes grouped with them include Samaritanism, Druze, Rastafari, and the Bahá'í Faith, she added, writing each name carefully. A student asked about Mandaeism. Ms. Park said Mandaeism is usually not called Abrahamic because its followers reject Abraham as a prophet. The class wrote careful notes before the bell rang. The room grew still as students compared the names on the board.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~125 words; covers all card facts.

story: Leo wanted to be a doctor, so he shadowed his aunt in a university lab after school. She told him anatomy is the study of the bodies of people and other animals, inside and out. Anatomists study the position and structure of body parts such as bones, muscles, and organs, she said, lifting a model rib cage. A person who studies anatomy is called an anatomist, she added, pointing to a labeled skeleton in the corner. They looked at a model heart and traced how blood moves through tubes and valves. His aunt explained that anatomy helps doctors and scientists understand how living bodies work. Leo left with ink on his fingers and a new plan for the future. He waved goodbye at the door.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~125 words; covers all card facts.

story: On clear nights, Nina and her grandfather used a small telescope on the porch. One evening he said an asteroid is a small rocky body that orbits the Sun in the inner solar system. Asteroids are like planets but much smaller, he explained, adjusting the focus wheel slowly. He showed her a chart where most asteroids orbit in a belt between Mars and Jupiter, a ring of dots on the page. A bright dot on the screen had a tiny partner beside it. A few asteroids have smaller moons called asteroid moons, he said softly. Nina drew the belt in her notebook and labeled it. Space, she decided, was crowded with rocks she had never noticed before. The stars seemed closer than before.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~123 words; covers all card facts.

story: For geography day, Tomas built a poster about Angola, officially the Republic of Angola, a country in southern Africa. He glued on flags and wrote that it borders Namibia, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Zambia, drawing lines to each neighbor. A blue strip along the west showed that its western border touches the Atlantic Ocean. In bold letters he added that Angola is the seventh-largest country in Africa. At the bottom he pinned a photo of a busy street in Luanda, the capital and largest city of Angola. Classmates asked questions about the coast and the capital. Tomas answered every one from his notes and felt proud of his work. His teacher gave him a gold star for the neat border.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~123 words; covers all card facts.

story: Rain soaked the trail, so Sam laced up his boots before the hike with his dad. A boot is footwear that protects the foot and ankle, his dad said, checking the fit around Sam's heel. Boots are higher and larger than shoes and sandals, he added, tapping Sam's calf through the fabric. These boots were high enough to protect the calves as well, which mattered on the muddy path ahead. Sam pulled the laces tight because boots may be held on with laces or straps. At a rocky stream, his dad pointed to the thick tread. Many boots have a strong sole to protect the bottom of the foot, he said. Sam stepped across without a slip. They hiked on into the wet pine woods.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~125 words; covers all card facts.

story: In art class, Ms. Ruiz held up a feather and a lump of charcoal while students settled into their seats. In light, black is the absence of all color, she said, switching off a lamp so the window glowed. In painting, black pigment can be made by mixing other colors, she showed on a palette with a knife. On a coat of arms handout, she circled a dark shape near a silver lion. In heraldry, black is called sable, she told them, writing the word in neat script. Then she placed white paper beside the charcoal stick. Black is the opposite of white, she said. The students mixed, labeled, and pinned their squares to the wall. The wall of squares looked bold and simple.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~124 words; covers all card facts.

story: After school, Jade met friends at the library cafe with hot chocolate. To chat is to talk about ordinary things that are not very important, her brother had said that morning, and now she understood. Jade chatted with one friend about homework, then joined a larger table by the window. A person can chat with one other person or with a group, she thought, laughing at a silly story about a lost umbrella. Later, her cousin sent memes from another city. Online chat lets many people send messages at the same time on the Internet. They used a messaging app on their phones. People chat in chat rooms or messaging apps on phones and computers every day, Jade realized. She walked home smiling at her buzzing phone.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~127 words; covers all card facts.

story: For a media project, Eli read about an unusual site in the school library. Time Cube was a personal website created in 1997 by Otis Eugene Ray, the article said. On the site, Ray described a theory he called Time Cube. He claimed Earth has cubic symmetry and that time rotates through four corners, which confused Eli at first. He also claimed that modern physics is wrong, the page insisted in loud capital letters. Eli's teacher reminded the class that scientists rejected these ideas because they cannot be tested. Eli made a slide that separated Ray's claims from real science. The project was strange, but it showed why testable evidence matters in research. Eli closed the laptop and saved his slides for class.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~123 words; covers all card facts.

story: Dr. Nia gave a talk at the aquarium about a huge research effort that filled the hall. The Census of Marine Life was a ten-year survey of ocean life that began in 2000, she said, showing a timeline. Researchers from more than seventy countries contributed data to the project, she added, pointing to a world map full of pins. The project cost over one billion U.S. dollars, but the team found thousands of species new to the records. Ron O'Dor of Dalhousie University in Canada led the effort, she said, pointing to his photo on the slide. A child asked how long ten years feels underwater. Dr. Nia smiled and said science takes patience and teamwork. Families lined up to thank her after the talk.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~125 words; covers all card facts.

story: On the farm tour, Mr. Webb held an ear of maize in his sunburned hands. Maize, also called corn in some countries, is a cereal grain in the grass family, he said, pulling back the husk. People first grew maize in ancient Central America, long before modern tractors rolled through these fields. About one billion tonnes of maize are harvested every year, he told the group, which made the children whisper in surprise. Most maize is used for animal feed, ethanol, starch, and syrup rather than direct human food, he explained. The kids looked at cows in a nearby field chewing calmly. Mr. Webb said the grain in their feed might have started in the same kind of row they were walking through.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~123 words; covers all card facts.

story: In the language club, Priya found a thin book on the shelf behind the dictionaries. Dutton Speedwords is a made-up language written by Reginald John Garfield Dutton, the cover said in faded gold letters. The idea of Dutton Speedwords is to make frequent words short, and very frequent words very short, her teacher explained with a quick demo. They tried writing hello and thank you in tiny symbols at their desks. Dutton Speedwords can be used as a second language for international communications, the teacher added, passing around a chart. It is also a shorthand writing system, which means you can use it to write quickly. Priya filled a page with swift marks and grinned at her friend. The bell rang before she finished the page.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~126 words; covers all card facts.

story: Coach Reed marked a track with chalk while the team stretched in the cool air. Distance is how far one thing is from another thing, she said, pointing from the start line to the far turn. Distance is also a measure of the space between two things, she added, stepping off ten meters. Distance can be measured along any path, not only a straight line, she told them. She told Mia to jog one full lap at an easy pace. Someone who walks in a circle travels a distance even if their ending position is unchanged, Coach said when Mia returned breathless to the same chalk mark. Mia checked her watch and finally understood the homework problem. The team cheered as the lesson clicked.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~124 words; covers all card facts.

story: At the rail museum, Omar climbed into a locomotive cab and gripped a metal rail. A guide explained that a diesel-electric engine is a diesel generator, a diesel engine that drives an electric generator. The generator feeds electric power to an electric motor which turns a driveshaft, he said, tapping a diagram taped to the wall. Its efficiency is higher than when an engine drives a shaft through gears, he added, tracing the path with his finger. Omar heard a low rumble from the yard outside. Most locomotives and many ships use diesel-electric drive, the guide said, nodding toward the window. Omar imagined a huge ship crossing the ocean on the same quiet power. He promised to read more about ships that night.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~123 words; covers all card facts.

story: During editing hour, Ms. Bell circled a sloppy ending on the board while pencils scratched. Et cetera means and the rest in Latin, she told the class, writing the phrase in full. It is often used in English to shorten a longer list when writers do not need every item. People usually write et cetera as etc., she said, writing both forms side by side. Then she crossed out ect on a sample paper with a red pen. Writing ect is incorrect because it does not abbreviate et cetera properly, she explained patiently. Students fixed their lists before recess. One boy kept etc. in his story about camping gear, tents, boots, and so on. Ms. Bell nodded approval. The room smelled like pencil shavings and paper.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~126 words; covers all card facts.

story: Zoe spent a week helping at the school paper after classes ended. An editor is a person who makes changes to documents or texts, the advisor said on day one, handing her a style sheet. A newspaper or magazine editor prepares articles and may choose which ones to publish, she learned while sorting drafts. Zoe trimmed a long interview and picked two photos that fit the page. The lead editor of a publication is called the editor-in-chief, the advisor noted, marking a headline in blue ink. Before printing, copy editors check spelling, grammar, and clarity, Zoe saw when she read the final proofs. She found a typo in the headline and fixed it. The paper came out clean and bright.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~120 words; covers all card facts.

story: In economics class, Mr. Shah drew two columns on the board and capped his marker. Financial capital is money and other assets used in business and trade, he began, listing examples. It has value because people agree it can be exchanged for goods or services, he said, pointing to a dollar and a stock chart. Money, stocks, and bonds are examples of financial capital, he added, writing each on the left side. A student asked if cash builds chairs by itself. Mr. Shah shook his head slowly. Financial capital does not produce goods by itself; it represents stored value. The class traced how savings might later buy tools and pay workers. The lesson ended with quiet pencils moving. Mr. Shah collected the worksheets at the door.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~126 words; covers all card facts.

story: From the pier, Lena watched fishing boats rock in calm water under gray morning clouds. A harbor is a sheltered place where ships can anchor safely, her uncle said, pointing to the breakwater. Many harbors are also ports where ships load and unload cargo, he added, gesturing at cranes and stacked boxes. They walked past trucks waiting in line. Ports have piers or quays where ships tie up, he pointed out, tapping a thick rope on a bollard. Goods from ports move inland by road, rail, pipeline, or smaller river ships, he explained as a train whistle sounded. Lena drew the harbor in her journal before the fog rolled in. Seagulls cried overhead as the boats bumped gently against the pier.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~121 words; covers all card facts.

story: On vacation, the family studied a map of the Pacific at the kitchen table. The Island of Hawaiʻi is the largest Hawaiian island and the southernmost one, Dad read aloud, tracing the chain. The widest part of the island is ninety-three miles across, he added, measuring with his thumb. The Big Island has more than half of the land area of the State of Hawaii, the guidebook said on the open page. Their hotel sat on a black sand beach that glittered in the sun. The island is part of the County of Hawaii, Mom noted from a brochure she had picked up at the airport. They planned a drive from lava fields to green valleys the next day. The map stayed open on the table all evening.
notes: Gold SFT story; ~128 words; covers all card facts.
